clinicalPearls: A milder allelic variant of Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome caused by hypomorphic missense mutations in the WAS gene that retain partial WAS protein expression.
Cardinal feature is congenital microthrombocytopenia: a low platelet count with characteristically small platelet volume.
Bleeding is usually mild, with petechiae, bruising and epistaxis, in contrast to the severe eczema and profound immunodeficiency of classic Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome.
Eczema and infections are absent or mild, but immune dysregulation and autoimmunity can still occur over time.
Small platelet size distinguishes it from immune thrombocytopenia, where platelets are normal or large, and helps avoid unnecessary immunosuppression or splenectomy.
The WAS protein regulates actin cytoskeletal remodelling in haematopoietic cells; the degree of residual function correlates inversely with disease severity.
Even in this attenuated form there is a lifelong, if lower, risk of autoimmune complications and lymphoid malignancy requiring surveillance.
Splenectomy raises the platelet count but increases sepsis risk and is used cautiously; haematopoietic stem cell transplantation is curative and considered in severe cases.
reference.pathophysiology: X-linked thrombocytopenia is caused by mutations in the WAS gene on the X chromosome that encode Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome protein, a regulator of actin polymerisation in haematopoietic cells acting downstream of Rho-family GTPases. Hypomorphic (usually missense) mutations preserve some residual protein and function, producing the attenuated phenotype rather than the null mutations that cause classic Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome. Defective cytoskeletal remodelling impairs megakaryocyte platelet production and shortens platelet survival, and it disturbs the immunological synapse, cell migration and regulatory T-cell function. The result is microthrombocytopenia with relatively preserved immunity, though residual defects in immune regulation still predispose to autoimmunity and malignancy.
additionalDifferentials: X-linked thrombocytopenia with dyserythropoietic anaemia (GATA1 mutation)
Inherited thrombocytopenias with normal platelet size
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count with mean platelet volume showing small platelets
Peripheral blood film for platelet size and morphology
Flow cytometry for WAS protein expression in leucocytes
WAS gene sequencing to confirm hypomorphic mutation
Immunoglobulin levels and specific antibody responses
Lymphocyte subset analysis and regulatory T-cell assessment
Direct platelet antibody testing to help exclude immune thrombocytopenia
redFlags: Intracranial or other severe haemorrhage during marked thrombocytopenia
Emergence of autoimmune cytopenias or vasculitis
Development of lymphoma or other lymphoid malignancy
Progressive fall in platelet count or new eczema/infection suggesting phenotype conversion
reference.prognosis: Life expectancy is substantially better than in classic Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome, and many patients do well with supportive care, but lifelong risks of severe bleeding, autoimmunity and malignancy persist. Haematopoietic stem cell transplantation can be curative and is weighed against the milder natural history.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing the condition as immune thrombocytopenia and giving repeated immunosuppression or splenectomy.
Overlooking the diagnostic clue of small mean platelet volume.
Assuming the attenuated phenotype removes the need for surveillance of autoimmunity and malignancy.
Performing splenectomy without appreciating the lifelong infection risk in a WAS-related disorder.
Failing to test the WAS gene in a boy with congenital microthrombocytopenia and a suggestive family history.
references: Nathan and Oski's Hematology and Oncology of Infancy and Childhood, current edition
International Union of Immunological Societies phenotypic classification of inborn errors of immunity
management: Supportive management of congenital microthrombocytopenia, recognising the small platelet size to avoid misdiagnosis as immune thrombocytopenia and needless immunosuppression or splenectomy
Bleeding precautions with platelet transfusion reserved for significant haemorrhage or surgical cover, and avoidance of antiplatelet drugs
Longitudinal monitoring for emerging immune dysregulation, autoimmunity and malignancy given persistent lifelong risk
Haematopoietic stem cell transplantation considered for severe or complicated cases, weighed against the generally milder natural history
Immunoglobulin replacement or antimicrobial prophylaxis only if humoral defect and recurrent infection develop
Genetic counselling for this X-linked WAS variant, with maternal carrier testing and family screening
Regular immunology and haematology follow-up with escalation for severe bleeding or new autoimmune features
